reader.title: Attempted lynching of the Corbett brothers
bases: Stockmen seized men accused of cattle theft, put ropes around their necks and lifted one off the ground before releasing them under an order to leave or be hanged (A4, A2, A1).

No one was killed: the accused were released with an order to leave within ten days (A4, A2, A5); it was an attempted lynching by a party of private stockmen acting on an accusation of cattle theft (A4, A1).

A telegraphic brief (A1), a condensed account (A2) and the Globe-Democrat story (A4) agree that cattlemen seized accused cattle thieves in De Soto county and nearly hanged them, though they may share one Florida source.

summary.text: The attempted lynching of the Corbett brothers took place in south Florida in the spring of 1888, when stock owners of De Soto county seized brothers accused of stealing cattle and put ropes around their necks.
One brother was lifted off the ground before the cattlemen relented and gave the brothers ten days to leave the country or be hanged.
The story ran in papers from Texas to New Hampshire, mostly in the cattlemen's own telling.

According to a Globe-Democrat account, stockmen in the southern part of De Soto county had for several months suffered from a "well-organized band of cow thieves" based in Lee county, opposite Fort Myers.
The thieves were said to change the marks and brands of beef cattle and drive them to Fort Myers and Punta Rassa for sale to buyers for the Key West market.
Informants in Fort Myers told the cattlemen that the Corbett brothers were bringing in cattle with "bloody ears and poorly disguised brands," and the account called them the leaders of the thefts.
Shortly before mid-April 1888, a party of the principal stock owners surprised the Corbetts at their home before daybreak and demanded an explanation of the charges.
The brothers took up their guns and tried to ride away, but they surrendered after several shots were fired; a shorter version says they were caught after a half hour's chase.
The stockmen placed ropes around their necks and prepared to hang them from a water oak.
One man was "actually pulled off of the ground" before, in the Globe-Democrat's words, his struggles "awoke some pity and calmer counsels prevailed."
With the ropes still around their necks, the brothers were reported to have confessed to selling hundreds of stolen cattle at Fort Myers.
The cattlemen refused their request for more time and gave them ten days to leave the country or be hanged, and the brothers promised to go.
A Florida news brief of early May said the captured men had been "made to leave the country."
No report of an arrest, of charges against the brothers or against the stockmen appears in the coverage, and no officer is mentioned in any account.

The earliest report, a one-line telegraphic item in the San Antonio Daily Light on April 14, said the thieves had been "mobbed" and had narrowly escaped hanging by "the enraged cattlemen whom they had robbed."

The fuller Globe-Democrat story, headed "The Ropes Were Around Their Necks," was reprinted in the Lusk Herald of Wyoming on April 27 and the Phillipsburg Herald of Kansas on May 4, and a condensed version appeared in a "Criminal" column in Concord, New Hampshire, on April 19.
The Globe-Democrat account told the story from the stockmen's side, calling the thefts a "nefarious business" and treating the confession made under the rope as settled.
It closed by warning that it would "go hard" with the brothers if they stayed, "as the cattlemen's word here is the only law that is respected."
None of the reports gave the brothers' first names or race, and a Louisiana digest of Florida news named no one at all, placing the capture near Arcadia.
The Globe-Democrat story speaks of "the three Corbetts," while the condensed New Hampshire version refers to "the four Corbett brothers."
Only the Louisiana brief names Arcadia; the fuller account does not locate the brothers' home and places the gang's headquarters in Lee county.

accounts.label: Telegraphic brief
accounts.gist: A band of cattle thieves in southern De Soto county was mobbed and narrowly escaped hanging by the cattlemen they had robbed.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat story (cattlemen's version)
accounts.gist: Stockmen surprised the three Corbetts at home, exchanged shots, put ropes on their necks and lifted one off the ground; after the brothers confessed, they were given ten days to leave or hang.

accounts.label: Condensed account
accounts.gist: Four Corbett brothers fled, were caught after a half hour's chase, confessed with ropes around their necks and promised to leave within ten days.

accounts.label: Florida news brief
accounts.gist: Several cattle thieves captured near Arcadia narrowly escaped lynching and were made to leave the country.

framing.detail: The Globe-Democrat story, headed 'The Ropes Were Around Their Necks', calls the thefts a 'nefarious business' and 'wholesale steal', treats the confession as proof, and says the stockmen's word is the only law respected.
Briefs in news-digest columns report the near-hanging in one sentence, calling the men 'cattle thieves' without comment.
A New Hampshire 'Criminal' column ran a condensed version of the cattlemen's account.

conflicts.note: A4 says ropes were placed around the necks of 'the three Corbetts'; A2 says 'the four Corbett brothers' were implicated. Neither is a local report.

versions.value: Corbetts' home, unlocated; gang headquartered in Lee county opposite Fort Myers, thefts in southern De Soto county

conflicts.note: Only A5 names Arcadia; A4 does not locate the Corbetts' home and places the gang's base in Lee county.
